title: Mass Society and Mass Culture Theory

ctx-era.prompt: Imagine it is 1895 and a newspaper’s sales are falling; the editor consults Le Bon’s book. According to Le Bon’s picture of the press, what is the paper forced to do?
options: Put in heavier, more instructive articles to educate its readers
Follow the crowd’s changing mood and drift towards light, fast, news-heavy content
Move closer to the government line and steer the crowd
Ignore the crowd altogether, since the crowd does not read newspapers
ctx-era.explain: For Le Bon the press stands behind the crowd, not in front of it: it has given up imposing ideas and, because of competition, has become a news agency that follows every shift of public thought. The first option treats the press as a directing force, whereas Le Bon says the opposite. The third does not fit the text, which says even governments have to retreat before the crowd. The fourth has no counterpart in the text.

ctx-tocqueville.prompt: Imagine that in a neighbourhood the majority decides a contested question and those of the opposite view quietly stop arguing. There is neither violence nor a legal sanction. Which concept would Tocqueville most likely use?
options: Crowd contagion
The tyranny of the majority
The tutelary despotism of the state
Healthy consensus
ctx-tocqueville.explain: The pressure comes not from law or the state but from the majority’s moral power over opinion, which is exactly the tyranny of the majority of the first volume. ‘Crowd contagion’ is Le Bon’s mechanism and needs a crowd to be present. ‘Tutelary despotism’ is the order of the second volume in which a central power looks after people, and there is no such power here. ‘Healthy consensus’ contradicts the fact that the opposing view has been silenced.

people-cast.prompt: Put these works in the order of their first publication (oldest to newest).
items: Tocqueville: De la démocratie en Amérique, volume 1 (1835)
Ortega y Gasset: La rebelión de las masas, book (1930)
Kornhauser: The Politics of Mass Society (1959)
people-cast.explain: The order is 1835, 1890, 1895, 1930, 1959. The pair that is confused most often is Tarde and Le Bon: Tarde’s book on imitation appeared five years before Le Bon’s, but his L’opinion et la foule, on crowd and public, dates from 1901, after Le Bon. Ortega’s pieces appeared in a newspaper in 1929; the book is dated 1930.

people-tarde.prompt: Imagine that hundreds of thousands of people all over the country, who have never seen one another, read the same news site on the same evening and share the same anger. According to Tarde’s distinction, what is this group?
options: A crowd
A public
Neither a crowd nor a public, merely a statistic
A congregation
people-tarde.explain: For Tarde the criterion of a public is that bodies are apart and the bond is mental, which is the case here. The crowd option is wrong, because a crowd is defined by contagion spread through physical contact. Tarde knew no internet or news site; we are applying his criterion to today. ‘Merely a statistic’ ignores that the shared anger forms a mental bond.

claim-core.prompt: Imagine a country in which trade unions, associations and neighbourhood organisations have collapsed, while politicians address the public directly from the screen. According to Kornhauser’s logic, what is the main risk?
options: That crowds are innately unintelligent
That it becomes easier for elites to mobilise people without intermediaries, while elites stay open to instant mass pressure
That the state sets up a mild tutelage that keeps people like children
That the public organises itself too much
claim-core.explain: Kornhauser’s formula runs both ways: elites are accessible to mass pressure and masses are ready for elite mobilisation; intermediate groups are the buffer between the two. The first option is the argument of crowd psychology, not Kornhauser’s; he looks for the danger in the absence of social ties, not in mental inadequacy. The third is a mix-up with Tocqueville’s second volume. The fourth is the opposite of the formula.

claim-variants.prompt: Match each strand with its basic fear.
pairs: Aristocratic strand (Ortega type)
The rise of ordinary people pulls down elite standards and culture
Democratic strand (Arendt, Kornhauser)
Isolated people can be mobilised by totalitarian movements
Left variant (Marcuse, Mills)
Rulers control the media and distract and numb the masses
claim-variants.explain: The aristocratic strand fears the masses rising from below; the democratic strand fears atomised masses mobilised from above; the left variant treats the media as the rulers’ instrument. The commonest mistake is to throw Ortega and Kornhauser into one bag: both say ‘mass’, but one defends elite culture and the other democracy.

concepts-glossary.text: According to Tarde, what holds a crowd together is {{1}}, and what holds a public together is {{2}}.

options: physical contact
shared class interest
a legal bond
living on the same street
a mental bond made through a medium (e.g. reading the same newspaper)
an inherited racial spirit

concepts-glossary.explain: Tarde defines the crowd as a bundle of psychic contagions spread by physical contact, and the public as the mental bond of physically dispersed people; the place where the bond is made is the newspaper. ‘Shared class interest’ is the criterion of Marxist analysis, not Tarde’s. ‘Living on the same street’ would in fact turn a public into a crowd. ‘Inherited racial spirit’ belongs to Le Bon, not to Tarde’s distinction.

concepts-crowd-public.prompt: According to Tarde’s text, what is the basic difference between “the audience of a theatre” and “the readers of a newspaper”?
options: There is no difference; both are crowds
The theatre audience is a crowd gathered in one place; the newspaper readers are a physically dispersed public
The theatre audience is a public; the newspaper readers are a crowd
Both are publics because both consume something
concepts-crowd-public.explain: Tarde writes that even where the “public” of a theatre is spoken of, a crowd is meant; newspaper readers are a public whose bodies are apart and whose bond is mental. The third option reverses the criterion. The first is the very confusion Tarde wanted to correct. The fourth brings in ‘consuming’, a criterion that is not in Tarde.

assump-five.prompt: True or false: according to Kornhauser, mass relations arise automatically from a society having a large population.
assump-five.explain: False. Kornhauser writes that a large population does not by itself produce mass relations; what decides is the scale of activities: large-scale activities such as national organisations, markets, audiences and electorates ignore or transform community ties. Many students shorten it to ‘mass society = crowded population’, but the theory’s interest lies less in numbers than in the way ties are formed.

how-lebon.prompt: Imagine that at a rally a proposal that everyone alone would reject is accepted without objection in the crowd. Which of Le Bon’s three causes would he call “the most important”?
options: The feeling of invincibility that comes from numbers
Contagion
Suggestibility
Anonymity
how-lebon.explain: Le Bon calls the third cause, suggestibility, “by far the most important” and treats contagion as its effect. Contagion is therefore the most visible cause, but not the most basic. The feeling of invincibility from numbers and anonymity make up the first cause, which removes responsibility; it frees the person from his brakes, but suggestion decides the direction.

how-kornhauser.prompt: In Kornhauser’s entry, which group is named as cut off from communal ties but not yet incorporated into the new order, and as especially inclined towards mass movements?
options: Old-established professionals firmly tied to their local community
New migrants, new workers and the young and mobile
The elites themselves
Only the uneducated
how-kornhauser.explain: This is exactly the group Kornhauser names: people who have lost their ties but have not yet been fitted into the new order, less constrained and more restless. The first option is a tempting trap: those tied to the local community can also resent big organisations and be open to movements, but Kornhauser mentions them for a different reason (resentment of scale and change), while the question asks about those who have lost their ties. The educational criterion is not in the text.

how-media.prompt: Match each writer with the role he assigned to the media.
pairs: Le Bon
The press reflects the crowd’s opinions and follows them
Tarde
The newspaper turns dispersed people into a public mentally
Tocqueville
The newspaper is a remedy that gathers isolated people who cannot find one another for common action
Kornhauser
The media run mass arenas by offering the same standardised options
Left variant
Media under the rulers’ control distract and numb the masses
how-media.explain: The five roles look alike but the fears differ: in Le Bon the media trail after the crowd, in Tarde they build the public, in Tocqueville they are a remedy, in Kornhauser they manage the arena, in the left variant they are the rulers’ instrument. The pair most often confused is Le Bon and Kornhauser: one sees the media as the crowd’s mirror, the other as the masses’ manager.

ev-stpauls.prompt: Le Bon predicts that “an anonymous crowd loses its sense of responsibility and can do anything”. Which observation in the St Pauls data compiled by Reicher contradicts this most?
options: Police cars being overturned and burned
The crowd not crossing the district boundary after the police had withdrawn, stopping those who stoned private cars, and directing the traffic
The rapid spread of rumours
The event beginning in the afternoon
ev-stpauls.explain: Limited, targeted, rule-bound behaviour contradicts the picture of a ‘mindless, unlimited’ crowd. The burning of vehicles shows that violence was present, not that it was unlimited; it does not contradict Le Bon. The spread of rumours and the time of day are details irrelevant to the prediction.

ev-personal.prompt: Imagine a researcher who, assuming that “voters watch the media and are directly influenced”, runs a panel study and finds that most voters, when deciding, look to the views of those around them. Which assumption of mass-society theory does this finding contradict most directly?
options: The assumption that culture is pulled to the average
The assumption that intermediate groups have dissolved and individuals are atomised
The assumption that crowds are inferior
The assumption that elites move to manipulate
ev-personal.explain: Looking to those around you shows that intermediate groups (friends, neighbours, family) are still at work, which is the direct opposite of the atomisation assumption. Culture being pulled to the average and the inferiority of crowds are other questions; a voter panel does not measure them. Elites trying to manipulate is not contradicted by this finding; it can only limit the effect.

crit-groups.prompt: According to Kornhauser’s defence, what exactly do the theorists claim about primary groups?
options: That primary groups have disappeared entirely in modern society
That primary groups exist but, as they are isolated from the rest of society, lose their functions of meaning and support for the individual
That primary groups were never important
That the presence of primary groups increases the effect of mass communication
crit-groups.explain: Kornhauser accepts the criticism but refines the claim: not the absence of groups but the loss of their function. The first option is the ‘total atomisation’ claim that was criticised. The third is not something Kornhauser defends either. The fourth is the opposite of the conclusion of the Lazarsfeld line: groups do not increase the effect, they mediate and limit it.

crit-verdict.prompt: True or false: according to Reicher, the Bristol 1980 data are conclusive proof of the social identity model.
crit-verdict.explain: False. Reicher writes that the data are not ‘proof’ but a ‘strong hint’ for the theoretical account; he also says plainly that he treats only part of the event and that there were some civilian harms. A good reader counts a study’s own reservations as the theory’s reservations.

crit-powerful.prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate summary of the link between “mass society and powerful effects”?
options: Mass-society theorists put forward a theory called the ‘hypodermic needle model’
The assumption of an atomised audience feeds the expectation of powerful effects; the finding that the audience is tied to groups weakens that expectation
Lazarsfeld confirmed mass-society theory
There is no relation at all between mass society and media effects
crit-powerful.explain: The link is a chain of inference: if the audience is isolated, the effect should be direct and strong; if the audience is tied to groups, the effect is mediated. The first option is historically wrong: ‘needle’ is a textbook label attached later. The third says the opposite. The fourth ignores the logical relation between the two ideas.

today-one-step.prompt: Where exactly does Bennett and Manheim’s “one-step flow” claim depart from the two-step flow?
options: Opinion leaders are stronger than ever
Messages go, in targeted form, directly to individuals without a process of social mediation
The media no longer have any effect
Individuals no longer live inside groups
today-one-step.explain: In the two-step flow the message goes first to opinion leaders and from them to the others; in the one-step flow the intermediate step is skipped and messages are targeted directly at individuals. The authors say the influence of opinion leaders has weakened, not strengthened. ‘The media have no effect’ is the exact opposite. The last option is our exaggeration, not the authors’: they speak of individualisation, not of the disappearance of groups.

today-bubble.prompt: According to the Facebook study by Bakshy, Messing and Adamic (2015), what is said to limit exposure to cross-cutting content mainly?
options: The algorithmic ranking, more strongly than individuals’ choices
Individuals’ own choices, more strongly than the algorithmic ranking
Only the size of friend lists
The platform’s advertising policy
today-bubble.explain: The authors report that individuals’ choices limited exposure to cross-cutting content more strongly than the algorithmic ranking did. The first option is the very thesis that ‘the algorithm locks us in’, and in this study it turns out the other way round. The third and fourth options have no counterpart in the abstract.

today-lab.prompt: You observe that a wave of anger spreads quickly among users of the same view but does not pass to networks of a different view. Which idea does this observation fit best?
options: Le Bon’s contagion model, in which everyone is affected at once, regardless of identity
The idea that contagion is bounded by the limits of a shared identity or group membership
The idea that there is no contagion and everything is coincidence
Mass-society theory’s thesis of complete atomisation
today-lab.explain: Diffusion slowing at group boundaries fits Reicher’s idea that “the limit of contagion is the limit of identity” and the finding of Brady and colleagues (this pairing is our interpretation). Le Bon’s model predicts a contagion independent of identity. ‘Coincidence’ does not explain the observation; complete atomisation contradicts the fact that the wave spreads inside groups.

turkey-lebon.prompt: According to the article by Polat and Durmuş (2015), what was Abdullah Cevdet’s relation to Le Bon?
options: He was Le Bon’s guide on a trip to Turkey
He was an intellectual who translated many of Le Bon’s works into Turkish and was influenced by his ideas
He was the fiercest critic of Le Bon’s ideas
He worked at the same university as Le Bon
turkey-lebon.explain: The article argues that Abdullah Cevdet translated many of Le Bon’s works into Turkish and was influenced by his ideas (the information on the translations relies on Hanioğlu). The other options have no counterpart in the article; in particular the ‘fiercest critic’ reading is the opposite of the article’s emphasis on ‘a source of inspiration’.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question: “Whose mass-society framework has at its core the idea that elites are accessible to mass pressure and masses are open to mobilisation by elites?” The right answer?
options: Le Bon
Tarde
Ortega y Gasset
Kornhauser
exam-patterns.explain: The accessibility of elites and the availability of the masses is Kornhauser’s formula. Le Bon is known for crowd psychology, Tarde for the public and imitation, Ortega for the mentality of the mass-man. The commonest mistake in exams is that the student who sees the word ‘mass’ writes Le Bon, the first name that comes to mind.

summary.prompt: Which is the most accurate summary of this lesson?
options: Mass-society theory is a proven theory and shows the absolute power of the media
Mass society is a family of ideas that carry contradictory fears; the atomisation claim has been strained by the evidence, but the questions it asked live on
Mass-society theory consists only of Le Bon’s crowd psychology
Mass-society theory is the proven ancestor of today’s filter-bubble debate
summary.explain: Throughout the lesson you saw the two strands, the different roles assigned to the media, the findings against the atomisation claim and today’s echoes. The first option treats the theory as proven, whereas its basic assumption has been strained. The third reduces the theory to a single author. The fourth ties today’s debate to a proven line of descent; the evidence is mixed.

quiz.prompt: What is the basic difference between Tocqueville’s “tyranny of the majority” and Le Bon’s “crowd”?
options: In Tocqueville the pressure comes from the quiet, moral power of the majority’s opinion and needs no crowd in the street; Le Bon’s crowd is people who are together and move by contagion
They describe the same thing; only the names differ
Tocqueville speaks of the violence of crowds, Le Bon of the opinion of the majority
Le Bon defends democracy, Tocqueville opposes it
quiz.explain: Tocqueville speaks of the moral power of the majority that ends discussion once it has decided; neither a crowd nor violence is needed. Le Bon takes physical togetherness and contagion as his basis. The second option erases the difference. The third reverses the roles. The fourth is not true either: Le Bon keeps his distance from crowd power and has been called ‘antidemocrat and elitist’.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Ortega y Gasset’s “mass” is the name of the working class.
quiz.explain: False. Ortega defines the mass by quality: the person who feels “just like everybody” and seeks no special quality; the mass-man can come from any social class. The reading ‘mass = lower class’ is therefore a common error in textbooks.

quiz.prompt: Match the names with their concepts or works.
pairs: Le Bon
Psychologie des foules (1895): suggestion, contagion, anonymity
Tarde
The distinction between public and crowd; the laws of imitation
Tocqueville
The tyranny of the majority and individualism
Ortega y Gasset
The mass-man: a mentality, not a class
Kornhauser
Accessibility of elites and availability of the masses for mobilisation
quiz.explain: The pairs most often confused are Le Bon–Tarde (contagion or public?) and Ortega–Kornhauser (mentality or social structure?). Tocqueville is known for the power of the majority over opinion.

quiz.prompt: Put these works in the order of their publication (oldest to newest).
items: Ortega y Gasset: La rebelión de las masas, book (1930)
Lazarsfeld, Berelson and Gaudet: The People’s Choice (1944)
Kornhauser: The Politics of Mass Society (1959)
quiz.explain: The order is 1895, 1930, 1944, 1955, 1959. Kornhauser’s book appeared after both works of the Lazarsfeld team; that is, the idea of mass society went on being discussed after the personal-influence findings too. Ortega’s pieces appeared in a newspaper in 1929, but the book is dated 1930.

quiz.text: According to Kornhauser, in mass society elites are {{1}}, and masses are {{2}}.

options: accessible to mass pressure
completely cut off from the masses
never elected
open to mobilisation by elites
tightly protected by intermediate groups
hereditarily obedient

quiz.explain: The formula runs both ways: elites open to mass pressure, masses open to elite mobilisation. ‘Isolated elites’ and ‘masses protected by intermediate groups’ draw the opposite picture, that of pluralist democracy rather than mass society. ‘Hereditary obedience’ is closer to Le Bon’s emphasis on race, not Kornhauser’s.

quiz.scenario: Imagine that a large factory closes in a city. Most of the newly arrived migrant workers belong to neither a trade union nor a neighbourhood association. A leader starts a movement with slogans addressed from television directly to these people.

parts.prompt: In Kornhauser’s framework, why are these people considered suited to a movement?
options: Because they are innately unintelligent
Because they are cut off from communal ties but not yet incorporated into the new order
Because they all belong to the same class
parts.explain: Kornhauser counts people who have lost their ties but not yet joined the new order (new migrants, new workers) as inclined to movements. The claim of mental inadequacy comes from the Le Bon line. Class membership is not a deciding criterion here.

parts.prompt: Which question would a researcher from the Lazarsfeld line ask first?
options: Is it really true that these workers are inside no group at all, and through whom do they receive the message?
How many times did the leader appear on television?
How loudly do the workers shout in a crowd?
parts.explain: The Lazarsfeld line questions precisely the atomisation assumption: do people receive the message through friends, neighbours and opinion leaders? The other questions either just count media exposure or focus on Le Bon-style crowd behaviour.

parts.prompt: How does Kornhauser’s warning apply to this scenario?
options: These conditions alone produce a totalitarian movement
These conditions raise the risk but alone do not produce totalitarianism; other conditions are also needed
These conditions carry no risk at all
parts.explain: Kornhauser writes that mass conditions alone do not produce totalitarianism and that other conditions are needed. The first option turns the chain into a fate; the third assumes the theory says nothing.

quiz.takeaway: Mass-society theory draws a map of risk and does not proclaim a fate; and the first testing question is always: are these people really cut off from groups?

quiz.prompt: What does Raymond Williams’s sentence “There are in fact no masses; there are only ways of seeing people as masses” mean at best?
options: Crowds never gather
“Mass” is a way of seeing: nobody calls his own people ‘the masses’; masses are always other people
There are no people in society
The mass media do not really exist
quiz.explain: Williams says the concept of the mass names not a social reality but a way of looking; masses are always “the others”. The other options read the sentence literally and end in absurdity: Williams is discussing not whether crowds or media exist but how the label ‘mass’ works.

quiz.prompt: In Reicher’s Bristol 1980 study, which finding contradicts Le Bon’s prediction that “an anonymous crowd attacks anything” most?
options: The attack on police cars
The crowd not crossing the district boundary after the police had withdrawn, and stopping those who stoned private cars
The spread of rumours
The start at 3.30 in the afternoon
quiz.explain: Behaviour with limits and targets contradicts the picture of a ‘mindless, unlimited’ crowd. The attack on cars shows that violence was present, not that it was unlimited. Rumours and the time are details irrelevant to the prediction.

quiz.prompt: True or false: according to the Facebook study by Bakshy, Messing and Adamic (2015), algorithmic ranking limits exposure to cross-cutting content more strongly than individuals’ own choices do.
quiz.explain: False. The authors report the opposite: individuals’ choices limited exposure to cross-cutting content more strongly than algorithmic ranking did. The ‘algorithm locks us in’ thesis is weakened in this study. Still, since the study belongs to one platform and one country, it is not a final verdict.

quiz.prompt: Which strand best describes Hannah Arendt and Kornhauser?
options: The aristocratic strand: the mass destroys elite culture
The democratic strand: totalitarian movements mobilise isolated people
The left variant: the rulers control the media and numb the masses
None; both are against mass-society theory
quiz.explain: Kornhauser counts himself and Arendt, with Fromm, Lederer, Mannheim and Neumann, in the democratic strand: the fear is atomised people mobilised by totalitarian movements. The aristocratic strand belongs to the nineteenth century and the Ortega type. The left variant is built on the media and the rulers. The last option is wrong too: both are defenders of the mass-society framework.

quiz.prompt: What change does Bennett and Manheim’s (2006) “one-step flow” thesis propose?
options: A shift from the two-step flow of messages from the media through social mediation to a flow targeted directly at individuals
An increase in the power of opinion leaders
The complete disappearance of media effects
That individuals no longer live inside any group
quiz.explain: The authors discuss a shift from the two-step flow (media, opinion leader, others) to a flow targeted directly at individuals. The second option is the opposite of their thesis: opinion leaders are ceasing to ‘lead’. The third and fourth options are exaggerations; the article does not say them.
